summary: D197 is a 1-CU course on Git and GitLab with no exam: you pass one performance assessment which, as students describe it, has you carry out a series of version-control steps in a WGU GitLab repository (cloning, committing, branching, pushing, merging, resolving a conflict and tagging) and paste a screenshot of each step into the task's Word template. WGU's catalog describes it as the basics of publishing, retrieving, branching and cloning, with no prerequisites, and it sits in term 3 of the BSCS. Students report finishing in an afternoon to a day and a half; one passer warns not to clear the terminal until every screenshot is taken, another says the instructor webinars cover every step but tagging, and some commenters found merge conflicts the hardest part.
author: Dorian Acosta

assessment.type: Performance assessment (Git and GitLab task, evaluator-graded)
assessment.format: One task · Git commands in a WGU GitLab repository · a screenshot of each step in the provided Word template · no exam
details: No exam: one task that evaluators grade against a rubric. WGU lists D197 at 1 CU with no prerequisites, in term 3 of both BSCS 202412 and BSCS 202611 and in several other IT programs, and, besides the standard course-planning item, its one competency is implementing version-control processes that maintain source code.

The work, as students describe it: in WGU's GitLab environment, clone the provided repository to your computer, make and commit changes, work on branches, push to GitLab, create and resolve a merge conflict and tag a commit. Smaller steps include adding the output of git version to README.md and creating a folder (students call it the retrospective folder) and pushing it.

Evidence: each step's terminal output goes into the task's Word template as a screenshot while you work. One passer found the template first, and another recommends reading the GitLab how-to linked at the bottom of the task before running any command; the second also says cloning the GitLab repository set up most of the task.

Help: a Jan 2026 passer reports five instructor webinars in WGU Connect that walk through every step except tagging (course page → Course Community → Join WGU Connect → Resources → D197 Additional Resources). Commenters say they're recorded on Windows; Mac users report that Terminal works with small differences and that WGU Connect has Mac notes.
Time and grading: students report 3–4 hours to a day and a half of work, and a Jan 2026 passer submitted the same night and had a pass the next morning.

Integrity: WGU's catalog requires your own work, bars falsifying anything you submit, and forbids reviewing other students' completed assessments, so every screenshot should come from your own terminal and repository.
tips: Follow the task steps line by line and paste each screenshot into the template right after the command that produced it. Don't clear or close the terminal until every screenshot for that step is in.

Set your identity and editor before step one: git config --global user.name "Your Name", git config --global user.email you@example.com and an editor you know, such as VS Code with git config --global core.editor "code --wait", so a merge or tag message doesn't drop you into an unfamiliar editor. On a Mac, Git can't start VS Code until its code command is installed: open VS Code's Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P), search "shell command", choose the entry that installs code in PATH and open a new Terminal window.
Read the GitLab how-to linked at the bottom of the task before you run anything; a passer recommends it as the first thing to read.
Run git status before and after each step. It shows the branch you're on and what's staged, which heads off most mistakes, and it makes a good screenshot too.

Learn tagging from the Git book's Tagging chapter, since a Jan 2026 passer reports the webinars skip it: create annotated tags with git tag -a, and remember that git push doesn't send tags unless you push them explicitly.

For the merge conflict, change the same line differently on two branches, commit both, merge, then edit the file, delete the markers, git add and git commit; screenshot both the conflict message and the resolved state.
Git doesn't track empty folders, so put a file in a new folder before you add, commit and push it.
Don't overcomplicate it: it's a 1-CU course, and one passer's advice is simply to do each step exactly as written.

competencies: Course planning: review your Course Planning Tool report with your instructor and create your personalized course plan together.
The learner implements version control processes and solutions that maintains source code.

topics.title: Version control and Git basics
topics.eli5: Version control is an unlimited undo button with a diary: every save point records what changed, who changed it and why, and you can go back to any of them.
topics.detail: A version control system records changes to a project over time, so you can compare versions, restore old ones and let several people work on the same files. Centralized systems such as Subversion keep the history on one server, while distributed systems such as Git give every clone the full history, so most operations run locally and quickly and you can commit without a network connection. Git stores each commit as a snapshot of the whole project, linking to unchanged files instead of copying them, and names every object by a checksum (a 40-character SHA-1 hash by default), which makes silent corruption detectable. The repository is the hidden .git directory that holds the history, and the working tree is the checked-out files you edit; a commit is one snapshot with an author, a date, a message and a link to its parent; and GitLab is a web platform that hosts Git repositories and adds projects, groups, merge requests and access control on top.
points: Git is the tool on your computer; GitLab (like GitHub) is a server that hosts repositories and adds collaboration features
WGU's four basics map to commands: publishing = git push, retrieving = git fetch or git pull, branching = git branch or git switch -c, cloning = git clone
Distributed means every clone holds the complete history
Short commit IDs such as 24b9da6 are the first characters of the full hash
The .git folder is the repository itself; deleting it erases the history

topics.title: Installing and configuring Git
topics.eli5: Just as you fill in a name tag before signing a guestbook, Git needs your name, your email and your favorite pen (an editor) before your first commit.
topics.detail: On Windows, install Git for Windows from git-scm.com (version 2.56.1 as of Nov 2026), which also gives you the Git Bash terminal; on a Mac, running git --version in Terminal offers to install Apple's command-line tools, or you can install Git with Homebrew. git version (or git --version) prints a line such as git version 2.56.1.windows.1 on Windows or git version 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155) from Apple's tools. Settings live at three levels: --system for every user, --global for your account (~/.gitconfig) and --local for one repository (.git/config), and the more specific level wins. Set your identity once with git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email you@example.com, because every commit records them permanently; choose an editor with core.editor, such as git config --global core.editor "code --wait" for VS Code (on a Mac, first open VS Code's Command Palette with Cmd+Shift+P, search "shell command" and choose the entry that installs the code command in PATH, then open a new Terminal window); and review everything with git config --list --show-origin.
points: A step that asks for the Git version wants the output of git version, not a tag
--wait makes Git pause until you close VS Code's message tab; without it, code returns at once, so Git finds no message and aborts a commit or tag (a merge just keeps its default message)
git config --global init.defaultBranch main names the first branch of new repositories main (Git 2.28 and later)
git config --global pull.rebase false makes git pull merge when your branch and the remote have both moved; with no pull style set, as with Apple's Git, such a pull stops and asks you to choose
git config user.name prints one setting, and git config --list prints them all
Stuck in Vim because no editor was set? Press Esc, then type :wq and Enter to save and quit, or :q! to quit without saving

topics.title: The three areas: working tree, staging area and repository
topics.eli5: Think of mailing a package: the working tree is your messy room, the staging area is the open box where you place exactly what you want to send, and a commit tapes the box shut and labels it.
topics.detail: The working tree holds the files you edit, the staging area (also called the index) holds the exact content that will go into the next commit, and the repository (.git) holds the committed history. A file is untracked until you first git add it, and tracked files are unmodified, modified or staged. git add stages a file's content as it is at that moment, so if you edit it again you need another git add, and git commit -m "message" stores everything staged as one snapshot. git status lists staged changes, unstaged changes and untracked files; git status -s shows the same in two columns (staging area on the left, working tree on the right); git diff shows unstaged changes; and git diff --staged shows what the next commit will contain. A .gitignore file lists patterns, such as *.log or build/, for untracked files Git should ignore; it doesn't affect files Git already tracks, which you stop tracking with git rm --cached.
points: Lifecycle: untracked → git add → staged → git commit → committed; editing again makes it modified until the next git add
git status -s codes: ?? untracked · A new and staged · M modified (left column staged, right column not)
git add . stages everything under the current folder; git commit -a stages tracked files only, never new ones
git restore --staged file unstages a file; git restore file discards its unstaged edits for good
Git tracks files, not folders: an empty folder can't be committed until it contains a file

topics.title: Commits, messages and history
topics.eli5: Each commit is a dated page in the project's diary, and the log is the diary read backward, newest page first.
topics.detail: A commit records the staged snapshot, its author and date, a message and the ID of its parent commit, so the history forms a chain you can walk backward. Good messages are short, specific and written as commands that describe what the commit does, such as "Add contact section to index.html." git log lists commits newest first; --oneline prints one line per commit, --graph draws branches and merges as lines, and --all includes every branch. HEAD points to the commit you're on, usually through the current branch, HEAD~1 is the commit before it, and git show <commit> prints one commit's details and changes. git commit --amend replaces the last commit, which is fine before you push but rewrites history that others may already have pulled after you push.
points: git log --oneline --graph --all is the clearest single view of a repository's history
One logical change per commit makes the history easy to read and easy to undo
Amend only commits you haven't pushed
git log -1 shows just the latest commit
Every commit permanently records the user.name and user.email set when it was made

topics.title: Remotes, cloning, pushing and pulling with GitLab
topics.eli5: The remote is a shared filing cabinet: clone makes your own copy of it, push files your new pages in it, and pull brings back what others added.
topics.detail: git clone <url> copies a repository with its whole history into a new folder and names the source remote origin, and git remote -v shows its fetch and push URLs. GitLab's Code button on a project page offers two clone URLs: HTTPS, which authenticates on each operation (with two-factor authentication on, a token such as a personal access token with repository scope, or an OAuth credential helper, replaces your password), and SSH, which uses a key you add to your GitLab profile once. git push origin main uploads that branch's commits, and the first push of a new branch is usually git push -u origin branch-name, where -u sets the upstream so later pushes and pulls need no arguments. git fetch downloads new commits without touching your work, while git pull fetches and then brings them into your current branch: it fast-forwards when only the remote has new commits, and when both sides do, it merges or rebases depending on your pull style. If no style is set, as with Apple's Git on a Mac, that pull stops with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches"; git pull --no-rebase merges, and git config --global pull.rebase false makes merging the default. If someone else pushed first, your push is rejected until you pull and integrate their work, and GitLab automatically protects a project's default branch, which limits who can push or force-push to it.
points: git clone https://gitlab.com/group/project.git creates a folder named project
First push of a branch: git push -u origin working; after that, plain git push
pull = fetch + fast-forward when only the remote moved; when both sides have new commits it merges or rebases (pull.rebase false or true), and git pull --no-rebase always merges
"Updates were rejected" means the remote has commits you don't: run git pull --no-rebase, fix and commit any conflict, then push
GitLab groups hold subgroups and projects, and members' access flows down from a group to everything inside it

topics.title: Branches
topics.eli5: A branch is a bookmark that moves forward as you write, so a new branch lets you try a draft without touching the published chapter.
topics.detail: A branch is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit, and each new commit on the branch moves the pointer forward; HEAD tells Git which branch you're on. git branch lists local branches with an asterisk beside the current one, git branch -a adds remote-tracking branches such as origin/main, and git branch name creates a branch without switching to it. git switch -c name, or the older git checkout -b name, creates a branch and switches to it in one step, and git switch name or git checkout name moves to an existing branch. Git refuses to switch when uncommitted changes would be overwritten, so commit or stash them first, and git branch -d name deletes a branch that has already been merged.
points: Create and switch: git switch -c working = git checkout -b working
git switch - jumps back to the previous branch
New commits land on whichever branch HEAD points to, so check git status before committing
A local branch appears in GitLab only after you push it
git branch -d refuses to delete unmerged work; -D forces it

topics.title: Merging and merge requests
topics.eli5: Merging combines two drafts into one, and if they changed different parts, Git stitches them together by itself.
topics.detail: git merge other brings another branch's commits into the branch you're on, so switch to the receiving branch first. If your branch hasn't moved since the other one split off, Git fast-forwards: it simply moves your branch pointer ahead and creates no new commit. If both branches have new commits, Git performs a three-way merge using the two branch tips and their common ancestor and records a merge commit with two parents. In GitLab, a merge request proposes merging one branch into another so teammates can review the changes, discuss them and run checks before anyone selects Merge, which is how most teams keep the protected default branch clean.
points: Merge into the branch you're on: git switch main, then git merge working
Fast-forward: no merge commit · three-way: a merge commit with two parents
git log --oneline --graph shows a three-way merge as two lines joining
git merge --abort backs out of a merge that stopped with conflicts, before you commit it; once a merge is committed, there's nothing left to abort
A local merge reaches GitLab only after you push the receiving branch
GitLab's default merge-request method always creates a merge commit, even when a fast-forward is possible, like git merge --no-ff

topics.title: Merge conflicts
topics.eli5: A conflict is two people editing the same sentence in different ways, and since Git can't guess which version you want, it shows you both and asks you to decide.
topics.detail: A conflict happens when both branches changed the same or neighboring lines of a file, or one branch deleted a file the other edited. Git stops the merge with CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html and "Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result," and git status lists the file under unmerged paths as both modified. Inside the file, everything between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the version from the branch you had checked out, and everything from there to >>>>>>> branch-name is the incoming version. To resolve it, edit the file into the version you want, delete every marker line (each conflicted section has three), run git add on the file to mark it resolved and then git commit to finish the merge, or run git merge --abort to go back to where you started.
points: Markers: <<<<<<< HEAD starts your side · ======= divides · >>>>>>> branch ends the incoming side
Resolve: edit → remove the markers → git add → git commit
Committing a file that still contains markers is the classic sloppy resolution
To practice: change the same line differently on two branches, commit on both, then merge
VS Code's merge editor or git mergetool can help, but finish with the same add-and-commit steps in the terminal

topics.title: Tags
topics.eli5: A tag is a permanent sticky label, such as "Version 1.0," on one diary page, and unlike a branch bookmark it never moves.
topics.detail: A tag names a specific commit, usually a release, and unlike a branch it stays put when you make new commits. Git has two kinds: a lightweight tag is only a name pointing at a commit (git tag v1.0-lw), while an annotated tag is a full object with the tagger's name, email, date and a message (git tag -a v1.0 -m "First release"), the kind the Git book recommends for anything you share. git tag lists tags, git tag -l "v1.*" filters them, git show v1.0 displays one, and git tag -a v0.9 9fceb02 tags an earlier commit by its ID. git push doesn't transfer tags by default: push one with git push origin v1.0 or all of them with git push origin --tags, after which they appear under the project's tags list in GitLab. Deleting a tag locally with git tag -d v1.0 doesn't remove it from the remote; git push origin --delete v1.0 does.
points: Annotated: git tag -a v1.0 -m "message" · lightweight: git tag v1.0
Push tags explicitly: git push origin v1.0 or git push origin --tags
git push origin --follow-tags pushes annotated tags along with the commits they point to
Checking out a tag puts you in detached HEAD; create a branch from it if you need to make changes
A Jan 2026 passer reports the webinars cover every task step except tagging, so practice it on your own

topics.title: Undoing changes safely
topics.eli5: Some undo buttons erase the past and some write a correction note, and on shared work you always want the correction note.
topics.detail: git restore file throws away a file's unstaged edits, and git restore --staged file unstages it while keeping your edits (older Git versions suggested git reset HEAD file for the same job). git commit --amend replaces the last commit, handy for fixing a typo in its message before you push. git revert <commit> makes a new commit that reverses an earlier one, which is the safe choice once work is pushed, while git reset moves the branch pointer backward: --soft keeps the changes staged, the default --mixed keeps them unstaged, and --hard discards them. git rm deletes a file and stages the deletion, git rm --cached stops tracking a file but leaves it on disk, and git mv renames a file and stages the rename.
points: Already pushed? Use git revert, not git reset or --amend
git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged
git stash shelves uncommitted work so you can switch branches, and git stash pop brings it back
git reflog lists where HEAD has been, which can rescue commits after a bad reset
Read what git status suggests: it prints the undo command for each section

topics.title: Working through the D197 task
topics.eli5: The task is a guided obstacle course: do each step in order, snap a photo at every checkpoint, and don't leave until the photo album is complete.
topics.detail: One passer installed Git and found the Word template first, and another recommends reading the GitLab how-to at the bottom of the task before running anything and following the steps line by line; paste each screenshot into the template right after the command that produced it. A useful screenshot shows the command and its output, ideally with the prompt or git status showing which branch you're on, and clearing the terminal too early means redoing a step. Two steps confuse people: adding "the git version" to README.md means the output of git version, not a tag, and the retrospective folder is just a directory you create and push, which Git can commit only once it contains a file. Some commenters found merge conflicts the hardest step, and a Jan 2026 passer says tagging is the one step the webinars skip. The commands are identical in Git Bash on Windows and Terminal on macOS, though paths and windows look different from the videos.
points: Before step one: install Git, set your name, email and editor, find the template and read the GitLab how-to
One step, one screenshot, pasted immediately; keep the terminal open until the step's screenshots are in
Add git status or git log --oneline --graph --all to a screenshot when a step is about branches or history
Mac users: Terminal works, and WGU Connect has notes on where the Windows videos differ
One Jan 2026 passer submitted at night and had a pass the next morning

plan.focus: Install, configure and read the task
tasks: Install Git (Git for Windows from git-scm.com, or Apple's command-line tools or Homebrew on a Mac) and run git version.
Set user.name, user.email, core.editor (on a Mac, install VS Code's code command in PATH first) and pull.rebase false (so git pull merges), then check them with git config --list --show-origin.
Open the task, download the Word template and read the GitLab how-to linked at the bottom of the task.

plan.focus: Local basics in a practice repository
tasks: In a scratch folder, run git init, create two files, and practice git status, git add, git commit -m, git diff and git diff --staged.
Add a .gitignore for *.log, then try committing an empty folder and see why nothing happens.
Read the history with git log --oneline.
Create a branch with git switch -c working, commit on it, switch back and merge to see a fast-forward.
Commit on both branches, merge again and view the merge commit with git log --oneline --graph --all.
Change the same line differently on two branches, merge, and read the conflict markers.
Resolve it by editing, deleting the markers, git add and git commit; repeat once, then try git merge --abort on a third conflict.
Watch the instructor webinars in WGU Connect (Resources → D197 Additional Resources), checking the Mac notes if you're on macOS.
Clone a practice repository, push a new branch with git push -u origin working, and practice git fetch and git pull.
Make sure your credentials work over HTTPS (a personal access token if two-factor authentication is on) or set up an SSH key.
Read the Git book's Tagging chapter, create an annotated tag and a lightweight tag, and compare them with git show.
Push a tag with git push origin v1.0 and find it in the remote's tag list.
Try git restore, git restore --staged and git revert on throwaway commits.
Work through the task steps in order in your WGU GitLab repository, pasting each screenshot into the template right after the step.
Keep the terminal open until each step's screenshots are in, and run git status before every commit and push.
Compare the template with the task line by line: every step has its screenshot, and every screenshot shows the command and its output.
Open the repository in GitLab and confirm the branches, commits and tags you pushed are all there.
Submit, and keep the practice repository handy in case a revision is requested; experienced Git users can compress this whole plan into one or two sittings.

practice.q: Which command creates a new branch named working and switches to it in one step?
choices: git branch working
git switch -c working
git merge working
git push -u origin working
practice.why: git switch -c working creates the branch at the current commit and switches to it; git checkout -b working does the same in older syntax. git branch working only creates it, leaving you on your current branch. git merge working merges an existing branch into the current one, and git push -u origin working publishes a branch that already exists locally.

practice.q: You edit index.html, run git add index.html, then edit the file again and run git commit -m "Update heading". What does the commit contain?
choices: Both edits
Only the second edit
Only the first edit; the second is still unstaged
Neither edit, because the file changed after staging
practice.answer: Only the first edit; the second is still unstaged
practice.why: git add stages a file's content as it is at that moment, and git commit records what's staged. The second edit stays in the working tree, so git status still lists index.html as modified, and another git add would include it. A plain git commit never picks up unstaged edits; git commit -a (tracked files) or naming the file, as in git commit -m "Update heading" index.html, would record its current working-tree version, second edit included.

practice.q: git push origin main fails with "Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally." What should you do?
choices: Run git pull, resolve any conflicts, then push again
Run git push --force so your commits overwrite the remote branch
Delete the GitLab project, create it again and push your branch
Run git commit --amend to refresh your last commit, then push
practice.answer: Run git pull, resolve any conflicts, then push again
practice.why: The remote branch has commits yours doesn't, so Git refuses a push that would throw them away. Pulling fetches those commits and combines them with yours (resolve any conflicts and commit), after which your push succeeds. Because both sides have new commits, a plain git pull stops with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches" if no pull style is set, as with Apple's Git on a Mac: run git pull --no-rebase to merge, or set git config --global pull.rebase false once. Force-pushing would erase the other commits, deleting the project destroys the history, and amending changes your last commit without fetching anything.

practice.q: In a file with a merge conflict, which lines hold the version from the branch you had checked out when you ran git merge?
choices: The lines after >>>>>>> feature
The lines between ======= and >>>>>>> feature
None: Git discards your version and keeps the incoming one
The lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======
practice.why: HEAD is the branch you're on, so the block from <<<<<<< HEAD to ======= is your side, and the block from ======= to >>>>>>> feature is the incoming branch's side. Lines after the closing marker are ordinary, unconflicted text. Git never silently picks a side in a conflict; it keeps both and waits for you.

practice.q: You've edited a conflicted file into the version you want and deleted all the conflict markers. What finishes the merge?
choices: git push the branch to GitLab
git add the file, then git commit
git restore the file to save your resolution
git branch -d feature to close the merge
practice.why: Staging the file with git add tells Git the conflict is resolved, and git commit creates the merge commit that completes the merge. Pushing before committing sends nothing new, and deleting the other branch doesn't finish anything. git restore refuses to touch a file that's still unmerged ("path ... is unmerged"), and with --ours, --theirs or --merge it would overwrite your resolution. If you want to start over instead, git merge --abort returns to the state before the merge.

practice.q: You ran git tag -a v1.0 -m "First release" and then git push, but the tag doesn't appear in GitLab. Why?
choices: Annotated tags can't be pushed to GitLab; only lightweight tags are accepted there
Tags have to be submitted through a merge request before GitLab will list them
git push doesn't send tags by default; push it with git push origin v1.0
Tags show up in GitLab only after the tagged commit is merged into the default branch
practice.answer: git push doesn't send tags by default; push it with git push origin v1.0
practice.why: Tags are pushed separately: git push origin v1.0 sends one, and git push origin --tags sends every tag the remote doesn't have. GitLab accepts both annotated and lightweight tags (annotated ones are the recommended kind for anything you share), tags don't go through merge requests, and a pushed tag appears right away, whichever branch its commit is on.

practice.q: Which statement about Git tags is true?
choices: An annotated tag stores the tagger, date and a message; a lightweight tag is only a name for a commit
A lightweight tag stores the tagger, date and a message; an annotated tag is only a name for a commit
Both kinds of tag move forward to the newest commit each time you commit, just as branches do
An annotated tag can point only at the latest commit, so older commits can never be tagged
practice.answer: An annotated tag stores the tagger, date and a message; a lightweight tag is only a name for a commit
practice.why: An annotated tag (git tag -a) is a full Git object with the tagger's name, email, date and message, while a lightweight tag is just a pointer to a commit, like a branch that never moves. Neither kind moves when you commit, which is what makes tags good release markers. You can tag any commit by adding its ID, as in git tag -a v0.9 9fceb02.

practice.q: A step asks you to add the installed Git version to README.md. Which command prints that information?
choices: git tag
git log -1
git describe
git version
practice.why: git version (or git --version) prints a line such as git version 2.56.1.windows.1, the version of Git installed on your computer. This exact step has confused students into making a tag. git tag lists or creates tags, git log -1 shows the latest commit, and git describe names a commit relative to the nearest tag.

practice.q: You create an empty folder named docs, run git add docs and then git commit, but Git says there's nothing to commit. Why?
choices: Git accepts a new folder only when its name starts with a capital letter
Git tracks files, not directories, so an empty folder has nothing to commit
A default .gitignore blocks new folders until you add an exception for them
Every new folder needs its own git init before it can be committed
practice.answer: Git tracks files, not directories, so an empty folder has nothing to commit
practice.why: Git's snapshots record files and the paths that lead to them, so a folder exists in the history only when it contains at least one tracked file. Add a file, such as a short notes file, then add and commit again. Folder names have no case rule, there's no default .gitignore blocking folders, and running git init inside a subfolder would create a separate, nested repository.

practice.q: Which statement about git fetch is true?
choices: It downloads new commits from the remote without changing your files or your current branch
It uploads your local commits to the remote and moves the remote branch to match yours
It downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch automatically
It deletes your local branches whose matching branches no longer exist on the remote
practice.answer: It downloads new commits from the remote without changing your files or your current branch
practice.why: git fetch updates your remote-tracking branches, such as origin/main, and leaves your work alone, so you can inspect what arrived before merging it. git pull is the command that fetches and then integrates the new commits (a fast-forward, merge or rebase), git push uploads, and fetch never deletes your local branches: even git fetch --prune removes only stale remote-tracking branches such as origin/old-feature.

practice.q: A commit you already pushed to a shared branch introduced a bug. What's the safest way to undo it?
choices: git reset --hard HEAD~1, then git push --force
git commit --amend, then push
git revert <commit>, then push
Delete the .git folder and clone again
practice.why: git revert adds a new commit that reverses the bad one, so history only moves forward and teammates' copies stay valid. Resetting and force-pushing rewrites shared history and can destroy other people's work, amending changes only your latest commit (and rewrites it), and re-cloning just gives you a fresh copy that still contains the bug.

practice.q: Which command shows exactly which changes will go into your next commit?
choices: git diff
git diff --staged
git log
git status -s
practice.why: git diff --staged (also spelled --cached) compares the staging area with the last commit, which is precisely what git commit will record. Plain git diff shows unstaged changes, so it can print nothing even when changes are staged. git log shows past commits, and git status -s lists which files changed but not the lines.

practice.q: Which command makes VS Code Git's editor for every repository in your account and lets Git wait while you write the message?
choices: git config core.editor code
git config --system user.editor vscode
git editor --set code
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
practice.why: --global writes the setting to your user configuration, so it applies to every repository you use, and --wait tells the code command not to return until you close the tab, so Git waits for your message. Without --global the setting applies to one repository, and without --wait the code command returns at once, so Git reads the message before you've typed it and aborts the commit. There's no user.editor key and no git editor command.

practice.q: Branch main hasn't changed since you created working, and working now has two new commits. What does git merge working do when run on main?
choices: It creates a new merge commit with two parents that joins main and working
It reports a merge conflict and waits for you to choose between the versions
It fast-forwards main to the newest commit on working, with no merge commit
It deletes the working branch once its two commits have been copied onto main
practice.answer: It fast-forwards main to the newest commit on working, with no merge commit
practice.why: Because main's latest commit is an ancestor of working's, there's nothing to combine: Git just moves the main pointer forward, which it reports as a fast-forward. A plain git merge makes a two-parent merge commit only when both branches have new commits (--no-ff forces one, and so does GitLab's default merge-request method), a conflict needs both sides to change the same or neighboring lines, and merging never deletes a branch; you do that with git branch -d.

practice.q: Your GitLab account uses two-factor authentication, and pushing over HTTPS rejects your password. What should you use instead?
choices: A personal access token with repository write scope, or an SSH key instead of HTTPS
Your GitLab password with the current six-digit two-factor code typed directly after it
Your email address in place of your username, together with your usual GitLab password
Your usual password again, after adding --no-verify to the git push command
practice.answer: A personal access token with repository write scope, or an SSH key instead of HTTPS
practice.why: GitLab's docs say that with two-factor authentication on, your password no longer works over HTTPS: use a token (such as a personal access token with write_repository scope for pushing) or an OAuth credential helper, and an SSH key added to your profile avoids passwords entirely. Appending a code to the password doesn't work, the email isn't the problem, and --no-verify only skips local hooks. WGU's GitLab environment may handle sign-in its own way, so follow the task's how-to first.

pitfalls: Clearing the terminal too soon. A passer warns not to clear or close the terminal until every screenshot for a step is in the template; otherwise you redo the step.
Committing on the wrong branch. New commits land wherever HEAD points. Check git status or your prompt before every commit and merge.
Making a tag for "the git version." That step wants the output of git version in README.md, not a tag.
Trying to commit an empty folder. Git ignores empty directories, so a new folder needs at least one file before it can be committed and pushed.
Forgetting to push tags and new branches. Plain git push sends neither a new branch without upstream nor any tag; use git push -u origin branch and git push origin v1.0.
Leaving conflict markers in the file. Delete every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> line before git add, and look at the file once more before committing.
Getting trapped in Vim. With no editor configured, a merge or tag message opens Vim; set core.editor first, or press Esc and type :wq.
Rewriting shared history. git reset --hard, --amend and git push --force on pushed commits can wipe out work; use git revert instead.
Copying the Windows videos literally on a Mac. The commands match, but paths, terminals and installers differ; use Terminal and check WGU Connect's Mac notes.
Overcomplicating a 1-CU course. The task rewards doing each step exactly as written, not extra Git features; follow the steps line by line.

community.summary: Two posts, a Jan 2026 pass and an older one from about 2023, describe D197 as quick: about 3–4 hours of work for the Jan 2026 passer and a day and a half for the other. The Jan 2026 passer installed Git and found the task's Word template first, then pasted screenshots into it while working. The older post's advice is not to overcomplicate it: read the GitLab how-to linked at the bottom of the task first, follow the steps line by line and don't clear the terminal until every required screenshot is taken; it also says cloning the GitLab repository set up most of the task. The Jan 2026 passer points to five instructor webinars in WGU Connect that walk through every step except tagging; commenters note they're recorded on Windows, that Mac users found Terminal works with some differences and that WGU Connect has Mac notes, and some switched to a Windows PC to save time. Commenters on the older post cleared up two confusing steps ("the git version" means the output of git version, and the retrospective folder is just a directory you create and push), and some found merge conflicts the hardest part. The Jan 2026 passer submitted the same night and passed the next morning.
